context_blurb:
Every engine, power station and fridge obeys two laws of heat found in the 1800s. The first: energy is never made or destroyed, only changed in form. The second: energy left alone spreads out, and spread-out energy can do less work. So no machine runs forever.

Most chemists around 1800 took heat to be caloric, a weightless fluid. In Count Rumford's 1798 test at Munich, horses turned a cannon under water against a fixed blunt borer, and caloric's believers said the grinding squeezed heat from the brass. A squeezed fluid would run dry, yet the heat kept coming for as long as the cannon turned. What a body gives without limit, Rumford argued, cannot be a substance: heat must be motion.

In the 1840s James Joule, a Salford brewer, measured the warming as falling weights churned water with paddles, then mercury, and as iron ground on iron. Every method came close to the rate he found in water: 772 foot-pounds, or 772 pounds dropped a foot, for each degree Fahrenheit a pound of water warmed. So steady a rate, whatever the material and however the work was spent, showed that work and heat are two forms of one thing. Energy changes form but is never lost: the first law of thermodynamics, the science of heat and work.

Perpetual motion, a machine running forever on nothing, breaks that law. Overbalanced wheels swing their weights wide on the falling side, where a weight far from the axle turns the wheel harder, as on a seesaw. But the far-out side carries fewer of the weights, so the wheel swings to rest where the two sides' turning pulls balance. Over a full turn every weight rises as far as it falls.

In 1824 the French engineer Sadi Carnot showed that the share of its heat an ideal engine, free of friction and leaks, can turn into work is fixed only by the temperatures of its hot and cold sides: the wider the gap, the larger the share. Steam near 540 degrees Celsius, cooled by a river, wins easily; on the sea's 20-degree gap a perfect engine turns only 6 to 8 percent of its heat into work.

Carnot pictured heat passing through an engine undiminished; Joule showed that work uses heat up. In 1850 Rudolf Clausius joined the two. An engine turns some of its heat into work and must hand the rest on to something colder, in a coal plant the cooling water of a river or a tower.

A gasoline engine is a heat engine too, working from the heat of burning fuel, so Carnot's limit binds it. An electric motor makes motion without first making heat, turning electrical energy straight into motion, so that limit does not apply and good motors pass on 90 percent or more.

Clausius's second law says heat never passes from a colder body to a warmer one without some other change. A fridge moves heat out of its cold box only by its motor's work, so its coils shed more heat than it takes in. With a fridge's door propped open in a sealed room, the pumped heat flows straight back in, and the motor's work ends up as heat too, so the room slowly warms.

Picture a ship that turns heat drawn from the sea wholly into work. Such a ship would create no energy, since it spends the sea's real heat, but it would break the second law: no engine working round and round can take heat from one place and turn all of it into work.

In 1865 Clausius named entropy, a measure of how spread out energy is; as it rises, energy becomes permanently unable to do work. Drive a long way on a full tank, park where you began, and the trip has used up none of the energy, but nearly all of its ability to do work. The energy still warms the air, too thinly spread for any engine to gather back; the fuel's atoms leave as carbon dioxide and water.

Entropy also gives time its direction. Run a film of a breaking egg backwards and the pieces leap up into a whole egg, yet nothing in it breaks a law: every bump between molecules works just as well backwards. But the pieces have far more ways to lie scattered than joined, so the reverse, though not forbidden, is overwhelmingly unlikely. Arthur Eddington called this one-way direction time's arrow in 1927.
